result: There is a particular hour before a city wakes when the streets seem to belong to no one. The traffic lights change for empty intersections, blinking green to amber to red as if performing a small ceremony for an audience that forgot to arrive. In that hour, the air feels different—cooler, cleaner, more honest. You can hear the hum of a refrigerator through an open window, the distant clatter of a delivery truck, the soft argument of pigeons on a ledge. It is not silent, exactly, but the noise has not yet organized itself into the day’s demands. I like to walk then, not because I am an early riser by nature, but because the world is briefly unclaimed. A bakery might already glow from within, its first trays sliding from the oven, and someone will be leaning against the counter with a paper cup, staring at nothing in particular. That stare feels sacred. It is the look of a person assembling themselves before the phone begins to ring. Later, the city will fill with errands and opinions, with doors opening and closing, with the bright, exhausting theater of being useful. But for now, the sidewalks are a blank page, and every small sound feels like the first word of a story that could still go anywhere. For a little while, no one asks anything of me, and I ask nothing of the morning except that it lasts a bit longer. I walk slowly and try not to ruin it.
